title: Making sense of the panic over Chinese AI
excerpt: On the latest episode of Equity, we discussed why Moonshot AI's Kimi seemed to panic Silicon Valley and Wall Street.
content_html:
The launch of the latest AI model from a Chinese company — Moonshot AI’s Kimi — reignited debates around American competitiveness and open versus proprietary AI.

While there was plenty of conversation on social media, it seems the debate is also happening behind the scenes in Washington, D.C., where OpenAI and Anthropic have reportedly lobbied regulators with concern about open Chinese models.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed why this seems to be such a hot-button issue. Beyond suggesting that certain folks should “touch grass” rather than spending their weekends arguing on X, Sean noted that in many ways, this “feels like we’re seeing repeats of prior freakouts,” with everyone in Silicon Valley “expecting that something is going to arrive and blow everything else away.”

And Kirsten noted that putting heavy restrictions on Chinese AI models could primarily benefit a handful of companies: “Are we accelerating and ensuring that Americans win the AI race, or are we ensuring that certain frontier labs do better than others?

Keep reading for an excerpt of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

Anthony: For folks who have followed the discourse around Chinese AI, this will probably be very, very familiar from the launch of DeepSeek, where basically a Chinese model comes out; on some benchmarks, it does as well, or at least seems competitive with some of the frontier models; and a certain portion of the tech industry loses their mind. 

Some of this [debate] got extra scrutiny because one of the people posting about it was [an executive] at OpenAI. But in general, there [is] this recurring question of: Can Chinese companies beat U.S. companies, at least in some aspects, and do it much more cheaply and in a much more open way?

Sean: Yeah, there are many elements of this that feel like we’re seeing repeats of prior freakouts. I think one of my favorites is: Everybody is so ready [for] and so expecting that something is going to arrive and blow everything else away. And I think my favorite example of that this past week was people showing off that “My gosh, Kimi made in 30 minutes an entire replication of macOS.” And yeah, it made a pretty impressive graphical reproduction of what macOS looks like, but it’s not an OS.

We keep seeing these things happen over and over again, where everybody’s so jumpy in the tech industry. And I think in particular, with some of the Chinese models that come out, there’s this expectation, and I think this gets to the core of why people reacted the way they reacted last weekend. (Also, by the way: Go outside, touch grass, it’s the weekend. Everybody in the industry was trading barbs on Twitter all weekend.) But this jumpiness is really interesting to me because we’re now a week out and I don’t think anybody’s feeling like the end is nigh like they were a week ago.

Kirsten: We have a really great story by one of our reporters, Tim Fernholz, who tries to unpack the psychosis around this here in the United States. He points to a number of reasons. And concludes — and I don’t want to conclude it for him, but I think that there’s one that rises more to the top than others. 

There’s concerns that these Chinese open weight models might have an implicit bias towards China, there’s another worry about security risks and guardrails. But there’s also a pretty big idea here, which is protectionism, and who is going to quote-unquote “win the race”? Is it going to be the U.S. or China? And that seems to be driving a lot of what the fear is. 

I don’t know, Anthony, if you agree with that?

Anthony: I completely agree. I think the China aspect always adds this certain level of hysteria. And that’s not to say that people shouldn’t be concerned about how the U.S. stacks up against China across different industries. But it gets so amped up.

The other thing this reminds me of is the discussion around TikTok a few years ago. And again, it wasn’t that I thought that the concerns around TikTok were totally made up, but that the level of how panicked people got — it seems as soon as you add the word China to any discussion, things just ramp up dramatically. And then in this case, it’s linked to this discussion about open [weights] and this idea that AI is so powerful and so dangerous that the only way we can control it is with these proprietary models from these American frontier companies. 

Obviously, most people saying this [have] reasons why they want to say that. David Sacks, who was the AI czar for the Trump administration [and] now has a different role in the Trump administration, was shouting on X about how, “I can’t believe people are opposing data centers, we’re tying ourselves in knots, there’s too much regulation.” And so it’s a way to argue for the positions that they already had around AI. “My gosh, if China beats us, that’s unthinkable, so you have to do what I want to do anyway.”

Kirsten: Right, and if you were to put across-the-board bans on Chinese open weight models — I’m not saying that there aren’t real concerns here, but let’s just play that out. If we were to do that, it would benefit models created by OpenAI, for instance, and it would force enterprises to use those as opposed to using models like Kimi.

So you really have to ask the question: Are we accelerating and ensuring that Americans win the AI race, or are we ensuring that certain frontier labs do better than others?

Sean: At this point, we should say a lot of this discussion really got kicked off by the head of strategic futures at OpenAI, Dean Ball, who was the first one to come out with this really long post mentioning some of these concerns.

Part of me thinks the reaction to this was because people disagreed with what Dean wrote. Part of me also thinks the reaction was driven by the fact that he kind of just said the thing out loud. He basically said the U.S. should create regulatory FUD — fear, uncertainty, and doubt — and muck up the ability for these open weight models to compete with the U.S. [Ball later backed away from this argument.]

And to me, I think you can read in some of the responses from folks, like, “You’re not supposed to say that out loud, Dean.”

content_html_zh:
一家中国公司——Moonshot AI 的 Kimi——推出了最新的人工智能模型，重新引发了围绕美国竞争力以及开放人工智能与专有人工智能的争论。

尽管社交媒体上有很多讨论，但这场争论似乎也在华盛顿特区的幕后进行。据报道，OpenAI 和 Anthropic 游说监管机构对开放的中国模式表示担忧。

在 TechCrunch 股票播客的最新一集中，Kirsten Korosec、Sean O’Kane 和我讨论了为什么这似乎是一个热门问题。 除了建议某些人应该“接触草”而不是花周末时间争论 X 之外，肖恩还指出，从很多方面来说，这“感觉就像我们看到了之前的怪异事件的重演”，硅谷的每个人都“期待着某些事情即将到来，并把其他一切都吹走”。

克尔斯滕指出，对中国人工智能模型施加严格限制可能主要使少数公司受益：“我们是在加速并确保美国人赢得人工智能竞赛，还是在确保某些前沿实验室比其他实验室做得更好？

请继续阅读我们的对话摘录，该摘录经过了长度和清晰度的编辑。

安东尼：对于那些关注中国人工智能讨论的人来说，这可能会非常非常熟悉 DeepSeek 的推出，基本上是一个中国模型的出现；在某些基准测试中，它也确实如此，或者至少看起来与某些前沿模型具有竞争力；科技行业的某些人失去了理智。

其中一些[辩论]受到了额外的审查，因为发布相关帖子的人之一是 OpenAI 的[一位高管]。 但总的来说，存在一个反复出现的问题：中国公司能否至少在某些方面击败美国公司，并且以更便宜、更开放的方式做到这一点？

肖恩：是的，其中有很多元素让我们感觉我们看到了之前的怪事的重复。 我认为我最喜欢的一句话是：每个人都准备好并期待着某件事的到来，并摧毁其他一切。 我认为过去一周我最喜欢的例子是人们炫耀“天哪，Kimi 在 30 分钟内制作了 macOS 的完整复制品。” 是的，它对 macOS 的外观进行了令人印象深刻的图形再现，但它不是一个操作系统。

我们不断看到这些事情一次又一次地发生，科技行业的每个人都如此紧张。 我特别认为，随着一些中国车型的问世，存在着这种期望，我认为这正是人们做出上周末反应的核心原因。 （另外，顺便说一句：到外面去，摸摸草地，今天是周末。 整个周末，业内每个人都在推特上互相吐槽。） 但这种跳跃对我来说真的很有趣，因为我们现在已经结束一周了，我认为没有人像一周前那样感觉结束即将到来。

克尔斯滕：我们的一位记者蒂姆·费恩霍尔兹（Tim Fernholz）写了一个非常精彩的故事，他试图揭开美国这里围绕这一问题的精神病现象。 他指出了一些原因。 最后得出结论——我不想为他得出结论，但我认为有一个人比其他人更能登上顶峰。

有人担心这些中国开放权重模型可能对中国存在隐性偏见，还有人担心安全风险和护栏。 但这里还有一个相当大的想法，那就是保护主义，谁会引用“赢得比赛”？ 是美国还是中国？ 这似乎在很大程度上加剧了恐惧。

不知道安东尼，你是否同意这一点？

安东尼：我完全同意。 我认为中国方面总是会增加这种程度的歇斯底里。 这并不是说人们不应该关心美国在不同行业与中国的竞争情况。 但它变得如此兴奋。

这让我想起的另一件事是几年前围绕TikTok的讨论。 再说一次，我并不是认为围绕 TikTok 的担忧完全是编造的，而是人们的恐慌程度——似乎只要你在任何讨论中添加“中国”这个词，事情就会急剧加剧。 然后在这种情况下，它与关于开放[权重]的讨论以及人工智能如此强大和如此危险的想法相关联，以至于我们控制它的唯一方法是使用这些美国前沿公司的专有模型。

显然，大多数说这句话的人都有理由这么说。 曾任特朗普政府人工智能沙皇的戴维·萨克斯 (David Sacks) 在 X 上大喊，“我不敢相信人们反对数据中心，我们把自己绑在了结上，监管太多了。” 因此，这是捍卫他们在人工智能方面已有立场的一种方式。 “天哪，如果中国打败了我们，那是不可想象的，所以无论如何你都必须做我想做的事。”

克尔斯滕：是的，如果你要全面禁止中国公开重量级模特——我并不是说这里没有真正的担忧，但让我们来解决这个问题。 例如，如果我们这样做，它将有利于 OpenAI 创建的模型，并且将迫使企业使用这些模型，而不是使用像 Kimi 这样的模型。

所以你真的必须问一个问题：我们是在加速并确保美国人赢得人工智能竞赛，还是在确保某些前沿实验室比其他实验室做得更好？

Sean：在这一点上，我们应该说，很多讨论确实是由 OpenAI 战略未来负责人 Dean Ball 发起的，他是第一个发表这篇很长的文章提到其中一些担忧的人。

我部分认为对此的反应是因为人们不同意迪恩所写的内容。 我也认为这种反应是因为他只是大声说出了这件事。 他基本上说，美国应该创造监管 FUD（恐惧、不确定性和怀疑），并破坏这些开放权重模型与美国竞争的能力（鲍尔后来放弃了这一论点。）

对我来说，我认为你可以读到人们的一些回应，比如，“你不应该大声说出来，迪恩。”
